paper_summary: Chordiya and Goel (2019) report a purely numerical LS-DYNA study of the drop weight impact hammer test on a polymeric syntactic foam (epoxy matrix with 60 vol% hollow glass particles and 5 vol% nanoclay), both as bare foam and filled inside an aluminium tube. Three foam densities (220, 320, 460 kg/m3), three drop velocities (3.13, 4.42, 6.26 m/s corresponding to 0.5, 1 and 1.5 m drop heights and nominal strain rates of 30, 40 and 60 /s) and two foam material models (MAT_063 crushable foam and MAT_024 piecewise linear plasticity) give 36 simulations. Peak stress and energy absorption rise with foam density and impact velocity, and filling the foam into a tube raises reaction force and energy absorption (about 4-12%) while lowering peak stress in the foam by 5-15% and reducing displacement.

extraction_notes:
This is a 100% numerical (finite element) paper - the authors performed no experiments on syntactic foam, so all 36 impact records carry data_origin='model'. The foam material card properties (density 220/320/460 kg/m3, E = 1.5 GPa, yield stress 30/40/60 MPa, Poisson 0.3, tension cut-off 8 MPa, tangent modulus 200 MPa) are taken by the authors from Gupta, Pinisetty and Shunmugasamy (2013) and are captured as 3 separate data_origin='secondary' records.

Unit conversions: densities 220/320/460 kg/m3 -> 0.22/0.32/0.46 g/cm3; modulus 1.5 GPa -> 1500 MPa.

energy_absorption_mj_m3 was left NULL for every record even though Table 4 gives energy absorbed. Table 4 reports total absorbed energy in joules (359-2345 J), not energy per unit volume, and the syntactic foam specimen dimensions are never stated for the main study (only the 80 mm dia x 100 mm aluminium foam cylinder used in the separate FE validation case is dimensioned), so no defensible conversion to MJ/m^3 is possible. The joule values are recorded verbatim in each record's test.specimen_notes and in its Table 4 evidence item so they are not lost.

strength_mpa holds the peak stress attained by the foam in the simulation (Table 3), which is the closest schema field; it is a simulated peak stress under impact, not a measured quasi-static strength.

Values NOT extracted as records: (a) the FE-validation case, which uses closed cell ALUMINIUM foam (570 kg/m3, E = 160 MPa) from Rajendran et al. (2009) - that is not a syntactic foam so it is out of scope; (b) hammer and aluminium tube properties (Table 1 and text) - not foam data, but recorded in specimen_notes; (c) all percentage comparisons (e.g. '12.34%, 12.76%, 9.08% higher reaction force') and the reaction force / displacement values, since the schema has no field for them; (d) numbers read off the 3-D surface plots in Figs. 11-15 (e.g. 200 and 500 kg/m3 interpolated points such as 7.816-16.78 mm displacement) - those are plot interpolations outside the three simulated densities.

Test temperature is never stated and was left null rather than assumed to be room temperature.
